notes.title: 잘 먹겠습니다
notes.text: Before eating, Koreans say 잘 먹겠습니다 ("I'll eat well"); afterwards, 잘 먹었습니다 ("I ate well"). It thanks whoever cooked or paid. Rice and soup are eaten with a spoon; chopsticks are for the side dishes.

notes.title: Five tastes
notes.text: 맵다 spicy, 짜다 salty, 달다 sweet, 시다 sour, 쓰다 bitter. To be polite about food you don't love, say 조금 매워요 ("it's a little spicy") instead of 맛없어요.

notes.title: Ramyeon after midnight
notes.text: Instant ramyeon (라면) is a Korean comfort food, often eaten late at night with an egg and kimchi, straight from the pot lid. In dramas, "라면 먹고 갈래요?" ("Want to come up for ramyeon?") is a famous flirty line from the movie One Fine Spring Day.

notes.title: "Have you eaten?"
notes.text: 밥 먹었어요? is a common greeting, closer to "How are you?" than a real question. And a Korean grandma will always offer more food: 배불러요 (I'm full) is the polite way out.

notes.title: Softening a request
notes.text: Add 좀 (a little) before 주세요 to sound softer and more polite: 물 좀 주세요 ("Could I have some water?"). You'll hear it constantly in shops and restaurants.

notes.title: Delivery culture
notes.text: In Korea almost anything can be delivered (배달), even to a park by the Han River. Jajangmyeon, black-bean noodles from Korean-Chinese restaurants, is the classic order on moving day or a lazy night.
